Learning Objectives

hereditary motor sensory neuropathy (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease).

sensory neuropathy.

neuropathy.

Hereditary, chronic, progressive peripheral neuropathies that affect motor and sensory
function
Typically, symptoms and signs progress in a distal to proximal fashion, most commonly
affecting the feet and hands
Caused by various genetic mutations with great variation in clinical presentation and
progression

Overview
Hereditary motor sensory neuropathy (HMSN), also known as Charcot-Marie-Tooth
(CMT) disease, is defined as a group of hereditary peripheral neuropathies caused by
chronic, progressive axonal degeneration. More than 50 different genetic mutations
result in HMSN. Patients have a wide range of phenotypic variations but classically have
weakness and sensory loss progressing in a distal to proximal pattern. Patients most
often seek treatment in late childhood or adolescence for the management of
symptoms, including cavovarus feet, intrinsic atrophy of the hands and feet, footdrop,
scoliosis, and hip dysplasia. Weakness of the proximal muscles is rare in patients with
HMSN, except in patients with the most severe disease. Currently, blood tests identify
approximately 90% of known mutations. Electromyography or nerve conduction studies
can be used to identify demyelinating HMSN.
Epidemiology
Most common hereditary neuromuscular disorder
Affects approximately 40 in 100,000 individuals
Most commonly appears in patients aged 0 to 20 years

Epidemiology
HMSN is the most common hereditary neuromuscular disorder. Prevalence is
approximately 40 per 100,000 individuals; however, this figure varies widely depending
on the population studied. Current estimates are that 126,000 individuals in the United

States and 2.6 million people worldwide are affected by HMSN. Men may have a slightly
higher risk than women; however, this difference is not clearly defined. Age at
presentation varies depending on causative mutation; however, patients most
commonly report symptoms between ages 0 and 20 years, and symptoms slowly
progress over a patient’s lifetime.1
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Affects the myelin sheath or axon of peripheral nerves
The most commonly affected muscle groups include the peroneal muscles; tibialis anterior;
hand intrinsic muscles, including the thenar muscles; and foot intrinsic muscles.
Weakness may progress to affect more proximal muscle groups in patients with severe
disease.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Because HMSN is a disease of axonal or myelin sheath degeneration, it affects the
longest nerves first, with progression of symptoms in a classic distal to proximal pattern.
In the lower extremity, the most commonly affected muscles are the peroneus brevis,
tibialis anterior, and foot intrinsics (including the extensor hallucis brevis and the
extensor digitorum brevis). In the upper extremity, the most commonly affected muscles
are the hand intrinsics (lumbricals and interossei) and the thenar muscles (opponens
pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, and flexor pollicis brevis). Muscles in the tibial and radial
distributions, as well as and more proximal muscle groups, tend to be relatively spared;,
however, they can may be involved in later stages or in patients with more severe forms
of the disease.
Etiology
Mutations leading to demyelination or axonal degeneration of peripheral nerves
More than 50 described mutations
The most common gene affected is PMP22.


Etiology
HMSN is a heterogeneous group of diseases that may be caused by mutations in
numerous genes that affect myelin formation and maintenance, cytoskeletal formation,
axonal transport, Schwann cell function, and mitochondrial metabolism. These defects
all ultimately lead to axonal degeneration that begins at the farthest ends of the axons
and progresses proximally over time. More than 50 described genes are currently linked
to HMSN. Mutations of the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17 account for 40% to 50% of
all cases of HMSN. Other commonly affected genes include GJB1, encoding for connexin-
32 (10% of all cases); MPZ; and MFN2. Most commonly, HMSN is inherited in an
autosomal dominant pattern; however, autosomal recessive, X-linked, and sporadic
mutations are described.2
Natural History
Most commonly appears in adolescence and slowly progresses
Normal life expectancy except in patients with the most severe disease
Variable severity and rate of progression

Natural History
The natural history of HMSN, including the age of onset, rate of progression, and overall
severity, varies greatly depending on type, causative gene, and phenotypic penetrance.
In most patients, symptoms begin during childhood or adolescence; however, onset may
occur at any age. Symptoms slowly progress in a distal to proximal pattern over years to
decades. The disease most commonly affects the feet first, and patients commonly have
pes cavovarus, claw toes, and footdrop. Later stages may involve the hands, with weak
grip and pinch strength, clawing, and visible intrinsic atrophy. More severe disease may
progress to involve the leg and forearm muscles. Scoliosis may be observed in 15% to
37% of children with HMSN, and hip dysplasia occurs in approximately 5% to 10% of

patients. Individuals with HMSN typically have a normal life expectancy because only the
most severe disease affects muscles required for vital functions, such as breathing.
Classification
HMSN type 1 (CMT disease type 1): demyelinating
Mutations result in demyelination of peripheral nerves.
Autosomal dominant inheritance is the most common.
Slowed nerve conduction velocity (<38 m/s)
CMT disease type 1A
Most common subtype
Duplication of PMP22 gene on chromosome 17
Onset in adolescence or early adulthood with slowly progressive symptoms
CMT disease type 1B
Mutation of MPZ
Same clinical presentation as CMT disease type 1A
HMSN type 2 (CMT disease type 2): axonal
Mutations result in axonal degeneration.
Autosomal dominant inheritance is the most common.
Much less common than HMSN type 1
Normal or slightly decreased nerve conduction velocity (>38 m/s)
HMSN type 3 (CMT disease type 3; also known as Dejerine-Sottas disease)
Rare, very severe disease resulting from demyelination
Appears at birth or during infancy with hypotonia, motor delay, ataxia or inability to
ambulate, and respiratory and swallowing difficulties
HMSN type 4 (CMT disease type 4)
Severe autosomal recessive form that may have demyelinating or axonal features
Onset of symptoms typically in childhood
Rare in the United States
X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT type X1)
Second most common form of CMT disease
Mutation in gene for connexin-32 protein, which is found in Schwann cells and plays a role in
myelination


Classification
CMT disease type 1 is defined as demyelinating disease and is the most common type of
HMSN, accounting for approximately two-thirds of all HMSN. Most commonly, CMT
disease type 1 is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion; however, rare X-linked
subtypes have been described. Patients with CMT disease type 1 have slowed nerve
conduction velocity (<38 m/s) in upper limb motor nerves. Most commonly, CMT disease
type 1 appears in patients aged 0 to 30 years and is slowly progressive. Patients report
pes cavus, atrophy of the lower leg muscles, frequent tripping, and ankle sprains. This
condition eventually progresses to involve upper extremity weakness. Although sensory
findings may be present on physical examination, patients rarely report sensory
symptoms. Subtypes of CMT disease type 1 are clinically indistinguishable and
determined on the basis of genetic testing.
CMT disease type 1A is the most common subtype of HMSN, caused by a duplication of
the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17. Overexpression of this gene leads to abnormal
myelin structure and function, ultimately resulting in decreased motor nerve conduction.
CMT disease type 1B is caused by mutations in the MPZ gene. More than 120 different
mutations have been identified, most of which are point mutations.
CMT disease type 2 is defined by axonal degeneration with an intact myelin sheath and
preserved conduction velocity. It is far less common than HMSN type 1. Numerous
genetic mutations result in CMT disease type 2 with no predominant pattern. Autosomal
dominant inheritance is the most common mode of inheritance; however, autosomal
recessive and X-linked modes also have been described. Electromyography shows a
normal or slightly prolonged duration of the muscle action potential. Clinical
presentation of CMT disease type 2 is similar to that of CMT disease type 1 in childhood
or adolescence. Patients with rare subtypes of CMT disease type 2 may have vocal cord
or phrenic nerve involvement, causing speech or breathing problems.
MT disease type 3, also known as Dejerine-Sottas disease, is a rare, extremely severe
form of demyelinating HMSN. It may appear at birth with generalized weakness,

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001038
6/18

arthrogryposis (distal contractures), and difficulty with breathing and swallowing.
Patients with less severe disease may present in infancy with motor delay and inability to
ambulate. Kyphoscoliosis because of generalized weakness is common. This subtype
usually is caused by spontaneous mutations of various genes, including PMP22, MPZ, and
EGR2.
CMT disease type 4 is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern and may have
demyelinating or axonal features. It is characterized by childhood onset of severe
sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Each subtype is caused by a mutation in a different gene
(several genes have been identified in CMT disease type 4), affecting particular ethnic
populations and producing distinct physiologic or clinical characteristics. In general,
symptoms of leg weakness develop during in childhood, and patients with CMT disease
type 4 may not be able to walk by adolescence. This subtype is rare in the United States.
CMT disease type X1 is the second most common form of CMT disease. This X-linked
variation is caused by mutations in the gene that codes for connexin 32. The connexin 32
protein is found in the paranodal region of Schwann cells, which wrap around nerve
axons and make up the myelin sheath. Affected males have clinical manifestation
between the ages of 0 and 20 years, with distal limb atrophy, weakness, and areflexia.
Females who are obligate carriers with one mutated gene often are asymptomatic.
Rarely, depending on mosaicism of the X chromosomes, some females may have clinical
manifestations but often with milder symptoms and later onset.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History
Extremely variable presentation
Common symptoms include difficulty walking, frequent ankle sprains, foot pain, and hand
clumsiness.
Family history may be falsely negative because symptoms may be underappreciated, and
presentation and severity vary.


Patient History
Patients most commonly report nonspecific symptoms of instability or difficulty walking,
lateral foot pain, frequent ankle sprains, and hand clumsiness. Sensory deficits are
variable and typically involve decreased sense of pain, touch, and vibration. Paresthesias
are less common but may be present. In patients with severe disease, hypotonia in
infancy, delayed motor development, or toe walking may be observed. Despite frequent
autosomal dominant inheritance, family history may be normal because of variable
presentation and recent advances in genetic testing for diagnosis.
Physical Examination
Highly variable physical examination findings
Lower extremity
Pes cavovarus (Figure 1)


Physical Examination
Pes cavovarus typically is the most notable finding on physical examination, resulting
from the tibialis posterior overpowering the peroneus brevis and the peroneus longus
overpowering the tibialis anterior. Pes cavovarus may lead to lateral foot pain or calluses
and wounds because of pressure points on the foot. Curled toes (hammer toes) are
caused by weakness in the foot intrinsic muscles, including the extensor hallucis brevis
and the extensor digitorum brevis. Footdrop (or, in patients with more subtle disease,
difficulty with heel walking) is caused by weakness in the tibialis anterior. Visible atrophy

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001038
10/18

below the knee may be observed in patients with more advanced disease. The tibial
distribution typically is the last to be affected.
In the upper extremity, patients may have weakness in thumb opposition and pinch
strength because of thenar atrophy. Finger clawing and abduction/adduction weakness
is to the result of atrophy of the lumbricals and interossei, respectively. Eventually,
forearm weakness may develop, primarily affecting the median and ulnar distributions.
The radial distribution usually is the last to be affected.
Motor symptoms often are more evident than sensory symptoms. Sensory changes
most commonly affect vibration, pain, and touch and progress in a distal to proximal
pattern. Loss of deep tendon reflexes often is notable on physical examination and helps
differentiate HMSN from other neuromuscular disorders. Although scoliosis and hip
dysplasia are less common, evaluation for these conditions during the clinical
examination is worthwhile.
Neurovascular Examination
Nerve conduction studies
Slowed nerve conduction velocity (<38 m/s) in patients with HMSN type 1
Normal or mildly slowed nerve conduction velocity (>38 m/s) in patients with HMSN type 2

Neurovascular Examination
Nerve conduction studies may be extremely helpful in confirming a diagnosis of HMSN.
Diffuse and homogeneous nerve conduction velocity slowing (<38 m/s in upper limb
motor nerves) indicates HMSN type 1 (demyelinating), whereas normal or mildly slowed
nerve conduction velocities (>38 m/s in upper limb motor nerves) with reduced muscle
and sensory action potential amplitudes are characteristic of HMSN type 2 (axonal).
Pathology


Pathology
Because of advances in genetic testing, nerve biopsy rarely is necessary to confirm the
diagnosis. If performed, biopsy may show various findings. Prominent myelin
abnormalities that resemble onion-bulb formations or myelin outfoldings may be
present in patients with HMSN type 1. Axonal changes from constant degeneration and
regeneration may be present in patients with HMSN type 2. In patients with some forms
of HMSN, nerve biopsy may be normal.
Diagnosis
History and physical examination
Nerve conduction studies
Genetic testing

Diagnosis
Approximately 90% of patients with HMSN are diagnosed via genetic testing. Because of
the high number of possible genes involved, testing typically is performed in a stepwise
manner, evaluating for the most common mutations first. In patients in whom genetic
testing does not reveal known mutations, the diagnosis may be based on patient history,
physical examination findings, family history, and nerve conduction velocity studies.
Nerve biopsy rarely is required for accurate diagnosis.

Differential Diagnosis
Entrapment neuropathy
Peripheral neuropathy secondary to diabetes mellitus, vasculitis, thyroid disease, B12
deficiency, excessive alcohol use, or other causes
Inflammatory and immune-mediated neuropathies
Certain distal myopathies

Differential Diagnosis
Many neuromuscular disorders may mimic the symptoms and physical examination
findings of HMSN. Patients with entrapment neuropathies, such as carpal tunnel or
cubital tunnel syndrome, may have similar upper extremity findings of thenar or intrinsic
atrophy and sensory loss. Patients with HMSN also may have concomitant compressive
neuropathy. Peripheral neuropathies secondary to diabetes mellitus, vasculitis, thyroid
disease, B12 deficiency, excessive alcohol use, or immune conditions typically are more
easily diagnosed based on patient history alone but should be excluded before a
diagnosis of HMSN is established. Most myopathies progress in a proximal to distal
pattern, differentiating them from HMSN. However, certain myopathies that primarily
affect the distal muscles, such as inclusion body myositis, myotonic dystrophy type 1,
and a rare group of distal myopathies (including Welander distal myopathy), may be
considered.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
No cure or effective pharmaceutical treatment for the management of HMSN
Physical therapy and home exercise programs
Lower extremity bracing
Full-length, semi-rigid shoe insole with first ray depression and lateral wedge for mild,
flexible cavovarus
Supramalleolar orthosis for more severe cavovarus

13/18

Ankle-foot orthosis for footdrop
Lace-up ankle brace if rigid orthosis is not tolerated
Upper extremity bracing
Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) blocking braces

Nonsurgical Management
To date, HMSN has no cure, and no medications have proved clinically effective at
halting or reversing disease progression. Several pharmaceutical treatment options have
been studied, including ascorbic acid, neurotrophin 3, creatine, and progesterone
derivatives; however, none has shown convincing clinical evidence of success. Initial
treatment for most patients with HMSN is nonsurgical, including physical therapy and
bracing. Exercise programs are safe and are the only treatment option with some clinical
evidence supporting improvement in walking ability and lower limb strength.
Management of pes cavovarus typically includes physical therapy and orthoses;
however, outcomes with these interventions are not well understood. Orthotic options
include a full-length, rigid insole with first ray depression and lateral wedge for mild
flexible cavovarus, a supramalleolar orthosis for more severe cavovarus, an ankle-foot
orthosis for footdrop, or a lace-up ankle brace if rigid bracing is not tolerated.
Nonsurgical management of upper extremity symptoms may include physical therapy to
improve synchronous flexion of the fingers and MCP blocking braces to prevent
hyperextension observed in patients with clawhand deformity.
Surgical Management
No agreed-upon indications for surgical management or treatment algorithm
Surgical management aimed at improving function
Cavovarus foot
Plantar fascia release
Tendon transfers


Surgical Management
Indications for surgical management are a subject of debate because of the highly
variable disease presentation and minimal clinical data to guide decision making.
Surgical management of HMSN is aimed at maximizing function and must be tailored to
each patient’s physical examination findings, risk for progression, values, and
preferences. Given the heterogeneity of deformity and severity among patients with
HMSN, no well-defined treatment algorithm is available. Preoperatively, the surgeon
must consider the effect of disease progression on the outcome of surgical
management. For example, tendon transfers involving the use a muscle group that likely
will weaken over time may not provide the best long-term outcome. Even after surgical
treatment, most patients will continue to benefit from exercise programs and bracing to
slow disease progression and mitigate symptoms.
Surgical treatment options for the management of cavovarus foot depend on flexibility
and severity of the deformity. Soft-tissue procedures, such as plantar fascia release and
tendon transfers, may be attempted in patients with a flexible deformity. Common
transfer techniques include peroneus longus to brevis, tibialis posterior to the
dorsolateral foot, and tibialis anterior to the lateral cuneiform. Bony procedures to

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001038

managed fixed deformity may include lateralizing calcaneal osteotomy and proximal first
metatarsal or medial cuneiform dorsal closing wedge osteotomy. Subtalar arthrodesis
and triple arthrodesis are reserved for patients with the most severe disease in whom
less invasive treatment options are not feasible or were unsuccessful. Outcomes of
these procedures are not well documented, and a high incidence of osteoarthritis has
been reported, even after arthrodesis.3
Severe claw toes may result in pain, difficulty with shoe wear, and skin breakdown.
Management of symptomatic claw toes may include extensor tendon transfer to the
metatarsal heads, flexor tendon lengthening, and interphalangeal joint arthrodesis.
Opponensplasty may be beneficial to improve pinch, grip strength, and thumb
opposition in patients with severe thenar weakness. Multiple variations have been
described in patients with HMSN, including transfer of the extensor indicis proprius,
extensor carpi ulnaris, and flexor digitorum profundus of the ring finger to the abductor
pollicis brevis and the extensor pollicis brevis. Despite limited clinical data comparing
outcomes, transfers involving the extensor indicis proprius or the extensor carpi ulnaris
seem to be most logical because the radial nerve is the last to be affected.4
For management of finger clawing caused by intrinsic muscle weakness, static and
dynamic stabilization procedures may be performed to correct deformity and restore
synchronous motion of finger flexion. Zancolli volar plate advancement or capsulodesis
stabilizes the MCP joint to prevent hyperextension; however, it may stretch over time.
This procedure can be performed in combination with various tenodesis techniques,
with the goal of bringing the MCP joint down into slight flexion. The Zancolli lasso
technique is a dynamic stabilization treatment option that harvests the flexor digitorum
superficialis tendon to the long or ring finger. The tendon is divided into four slips, and a
tendon slip is passed through the proximal pulley of each finger and attached back onto
itself.4
Outcomes
Little clinical evidence is available on the outcomes of nonsurgical or surgical management

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001038
16/18

Exercise programs have been shown to improve strength and gait.
Management should be aimed at improving function and pain.

Outcomes
Because of the heterogeneous nature of HMSN, clinical studies evaluating outcomes are
extremely difficult to perform and do not provide reliable data to guide management.
Newer, psychometrically supported scales have been developed (CMT Neuropathy Score
second version, CMT Disease Pediatric Scale, CMT Disease Infant Scale, CMT Functional
Outcome Measure, and CMT Health Index); however, most of these scales have not been
formally tested in longitudinal studies. Serum biomarkers have been identified; however,
their responsiveness to therapies remains unknown. Therefore, treatment decisions
typically are based on the severity of symptoms, the effect on function, and surgeon
experience. No pharmaceutical treatment options are available to reverse or slow the
underlying nerve degeneration that causes HMSN; however, exercise programs, bracing,
and surgical management may improve function.
Mark as Complete
